newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.African growth shows surprise fall in Q1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.African growth shows surprise fall in Q1.

text.p: South Africa recorded a surprise fall in gross domestic product (GDP) in the first quarter of 1997, confounding economists' expectations and sparking renewed hopes of an interest rate cut.
GDP fell a seasonally adjusted and annualised 0.8 percent in the quarter to March after rising 3.3 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996. Economists had, on average, forecast a rise of 2.5 percent.
Bond and stock markets reacted favourably to the news as dealers speculated the weak growth numbers would put mounting pressure on Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals to cut currently high rates.
"The number is good for an interest rate cut later in the year," said SBC Warburg economist Michael McClintock.

The GDP contraction was the first since the first quarter of 1994 and was mainly due to a decline in agricultural production, falling from a high base a year ago when excellent summer rains boosted output.
"It's bad for the economy but positive for bonds," said one bond trader as the local benchmark long bond yield fell 20 basis points.
The GDP data followed a mixed bunch of economic indicators on Wednesday showing inflation on the rise but broadly-based M3 money supply growth easing.

Stals told Reuters after those figures he had no plans to ease monetary policy in the near future. But he acknowledged the slowdown in the economy would eventually reduce inflationary, money and credit growth pressures, his main areas of concern.

"We are not going to come down (cut rates) soon, certainly. But we will watch it very carefully. The trends in real economic activity certainly indicate a slowdown and one must expect that these financial areas must follow sooner or later," he said.
Board of Executors economist Rob Lee this week accused the Reserve Bank of over-estimating the economy's resilience and urged it to stimulate flagging growth by cutting interest rates.
Warburg's McClintock, who expects two one point reductions in official rates in the second half of the year, saw the economy remaining weak but stopped short of predicting recession.

"I don't think the worst is over for agriculture yet, especially given the bad weather that we've had, and I think mining will do worse in the second quarter...If you take those factors into consideration your second quarter number is going to be pretty weak," he said.
Not all economists, however, jumped on the growth figures as justification for a rate cut.

"I don't think they should (cut rates) on the back of just one quarter's GDP numbers," said chief economist at Old Mutual Asset Managers Dave Mohr, who saw a rate cut only very late this year or in 1998.
"The slowdown is likely to continue but I think it will be a moderate slowdown. I don't see that we're going to get successive quarters of negative GDP numbers."

South African shares staged a mini-rally on the GDP figures, taking the all-share index to 7,065.2 points, up 24.4 points on the day, as dealers focussed on the potential for a cut in rates rather than the negativeness of weakening economic activity.
The benchmark R150 bond was last yielding 14.855 percent, having hit to an intraday best of 14.84 percent, from 15.06 at the local close on Wednesday.
South Africa's official Bank rate is currently set at 17 percent while commercial banks' prime lending rate is 20.25 percent, a real interest rate of over 10 percent after allowing for inflation.
